Note: uses the same University of Illinois recruitment protocol/admission criteria and formula brand as covidence #1882 (Wang et al. 2015), raising possible subject overlap, though the two papers analyze different outcomes (transcriptome-microbiome crosstalk here vs. HMO-taxa correlation there).

title: Microbial Glycoside Hydrolases in the First Year of Life: An Analysis Review on Their Presence and Importance in Infant Gut.
justification: The paper is explicitly titled and presented as an 'Analysis Review' synthesizing existing literature on microbial glycoside hydrolases in the infant gut, not a primary study with its own subjects.

title: Meta-analysis of effects of exclusive breastfeeding on infant gut microbiota across populations.
justification: This is a meta-analysis pooling previously published data from seven existing microbiome studies (1825 stool samples from 684 infants), not a primary study with its own newly recruited cohort.

title: Human milk oligosaccharides as a factor in forming differentiated microbiological profiles of the gut microbiota in infants in the first months of life (Russian).
justification: The only two study groups are breastfed (n=45) infants and formula-fed infants receiving formula fortified with GOS prebiotic and 2'-fucosyllactose (HMO) (n=45); no unsupplemented standard-formula control group exists, so an unsupplemented-formula-vs-breastfed contrast cannot be isolated.

title: Nationwide cohort study reveals low bifidobacteria and distinct microbiota composition and function in Swedish newborns.
justification: The study's exposure of interest is Bifidobacterium-presence/absence (foundational community types CT1-3), not feeding mode; the paper explicitly states breastfeeding practices did not differ between the Bifidobacterium-positive and -negative groups, and only 4% of the cohort was exclusively formula-fed with no separate taxonomic comparison reported against this group.

title: Maternal nutrition and its impact on neonatal immune development.
justification: Explicitly published as a 'Point of View' commentary/opinion piece synthesizing general mechanisms, with no original study subjects, methods, or data.

title: Characterization of gut microbiota in preterm infants at discharge: a single-center observational study.
justification: Cohort is 103 preterm infants (28-36+6 weeks) plus 32 term infants; the reported formula-feeding association with microbiota beta-diversity (R2=0.137, P<0.001) and taxa (Enterococcus) is computed across the pooled preterm-and-term sample rather than reported as a separable healthy-term-only breastfed-vs-formula-fed analysis.

title: Multi-Omics Profiling of the 42-Day Infant Gut as a Pilot Predictor of Atopic Dermatitis at One Year: A Birth Cohort Study in China.
justification: The study exposure/outcome is atopic dermatitis vs non-AD status at one year, not feeding mode; the only feeding categories reported are breastfeeding (12/18) and mixed feeding (6/18), with no exclusively formula-fed group and no feeding-based microbiota comparison.

title: Gut Microbiota Profile of Infants with Breastfeeding and Mixed Feeding Patterns.
justification: The study explicitly compares only breastfeeding (n=55) and mixed feeding (n=48) groups; no exclusively formula-fed group was recruited or compared.

title: Proof of principle study replicating microbial clusters in connection to birth mode and diet in the early life intestine.
justification: All formula-fed infants in this allergy-prevention RCT received hypoallergenic formula randomized to with or without added GOS/FOS plus pectin-derived acidic oligosaccharides (pAOS); the headline breastfed-vs-formula-fed maturation comparison pools prebiotic-supplemented and unsupplemented formula infants together, and the paper's own separate analysis confirms the prebiotic supplement independently affects maturation (p=0.025), so a clean unsupplemented-formula-vs-breastfed contrast is not isolated.

title: Characterization of the gut microbiota and systemic inflammation in HIV-exposed uninfected infants from a resource-limited setting at 6 weeks of age.
justification: At 6 weeks, 84.6% of infants were exclusively breastfed and 15.4% were mixed-fed with fluids/semi-solids; no exclusively formula-fed group existed, and the paper reports breastfeeding practice had no significant association with gut microbiota diversity or composition.

title: Maturation of the gut metabolome during the first year of life in humans.
justification: 152 healthy full-term Chinese infants (gestational age 37-42 weeks, no prematurity), stool profiled longitudinally (newborn, 4mo, 12mo) by V4 16S rRNA sequencing alongside LC-MS metabolomics; exclusively breastfed, mixed-fed, and exclusively formula-fed infants were compared, with formula feeding associated with increased C. perfringens abundance and short-chain acylcarnitine levels.

title: MFGM components promote gut Bifidobacterium growth in infant and in vitro.
justification: 44 healthy term infants (37-41 weeks gestation) randomized/assigned to breastfeeding (n=16), common unsupplemented formula (FF1, n=13), or MFGM-modified formula (FF2, n=15); stool profiled by 16S rRNA high-throughput sequencing at 1 month found breastfed infants had higher Bifidobacterium and lower Escherichia abundance than formula-fed infants.

title: Gut microbiome profile in zinc deficient infants using next generation sequencing.
justification: 46 healthy infants (1-4 months, Peshawar, Pakistan; no antibiotics, probiotics, or chronic illness), 23 exclusively breastfed and 23 exclusively formula-fed, stool profiled by metagenomic shotgun next-generation sequencing; reports differential Bacteroidetes, Proteobacteria, and Firmicutes abundance correlations by feeding group. No explicit gestational-age/term statement in the text, flagged as a borderline population call.

title: The Assessment of Fecal Volatile Organic Compounds in Healthy Infants: Electronic Nose Device Predicts Patient Demographics and Microbial Enterotype.
justification: The breastmilk-vs-formula comparison reported as statistically significant is for fecal volatile organic compound (VOC) 'smellprints' from an electronic nose device, not sequencing-based bacterial taxonomic composition; 16S rRNA sequencing was used only to define separate microbial enterotypes, which were not themselves reported as differing by feeding type.

title: Effects of Different Modes of Delivery and Feeding on Intestinal Flora of Newborns and Infants with Different Ages.
justification: 108 healthy full-term newborns/infants (no diarrhea, GI disease, or antibiotic use), stool profiled by 16S rRNA V3-V4 high-throughput sequencing; at 0-6 months, naturally-delivered breastfed (MV1) vs goat-milk-formula-fed (YV1) infants differed significantly in Actinobacteria/Firmicutes abundance and genus-level Bifidobacterium, Clostridium-sensu-stricto-1, and Bacteroides (P<0.05).

title: Perinatal factors affect the gut microbiota up to four years after birth.
justification: All faecal samples in this study were collected at years one, two, and four of age (none within 0-12 months), and the paper explicitly reports no significant clustering of microbiota by duration of breastfeeding, so there is no in-scope breastfed-vs-formula stool comparison.

title: Differences in the bacterial profiles of infant gut by birth process, milk diet, and choice of 16S rRNA gene target region.
justification: 60 healthy full-term Filipino infants (2-4 months), stool profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing; exclusively breastfed, formula-fed (80-100% formula), and mixed-fed groups compared, with exclusive breastfeeding associated with higher Bifidobacterium longum (P=0.0315) and formula/mixed feeding associated with higher Enterobacteriaceae and Veillonella dispar (P<0.05); a separate PCoA (Fig. 3b) directly contrasts vaginally-delivered breastfed vs vaginally-delivered formula-milk groups.

title: Human Breast Milk and Infant Formulas Differentially Modify the Intestinal Microbiota in Human Infants and Host Physiology in Rats.
justification: In the human infant arm (BF vs SPCF formula vs standard formulas), fecal bacterial composition was assessed only by qPCR targeting Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, and Clostridium perfringens; 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed only in the separate weanling rat model, not in the human infants.

title: The role of breast-feeding in infant immune system: a systems perspective on the intestinal microbiome.
exclusion_reason: Duplicate report of an already-included cohort
justification: This paper explicitly reanalyzes the identical metagenomic (EBI SRA ERP001038) and transcriptomic (GEO GSE31075) dataset from the same breastfed/formula-fed infants as Schwartz et al. 2012 (covidence #2022, already included), applying a systems-biology network analysis rather than collecting any new primary data.

title: Development of the gut microbiota and mucosal IgA responses in twins and gnotobiotic mice.
justification: This is a cohort of 40 twin pairs; twin gestations carry a well-documented substantially elevated risk of preterm birth, and the paper reports no gestational-age data or term-only restriction/separable term subgroup for its V4-16S rRNA breastfed-vs-formula-fed microbiota maturity comparison (consistent with the same population concern applied to covidence #1527, another twin cohort with confirmed near-50% sub-37-week gestational ages).

title: Impact of Diet in Shaping Gut Microbiota Revealed by a Comparative Study in Infants During the First Six Months of Life.
justification: Duplicate Covidence record of the same paper as covidence #1948 (same paper_id/manuscript); decision replicated: 24 healthy term infants (37-42 weeks gestation) divided into breast-fed, mixed-fed, and exclusively formula-fed groups, 16S rDNA pyrosequencing found FF infants had significantly depleted Bacteroidetes/Actinobacteria and higher Enterobacteriaceae, with Bifidobacteriaceae significantly higher in BF (19.15%) than FF (4.04%).

title: Starter formula enriched in prebiotics and probiotics ensures normal growth of infants and promotes gut health: a randomized clinical trial.
justification: Duplicate Covidence record of the same paper as covidence #1720 (same paper_id/manuscript); decision replicated: fecal bacterial analysis was performed by FISH and culture-based bacteriological counts, not sequencing-based taxonomic profiling.

title: Physiological and Bifidogenic Effects of Prebiotic Supplements in Infant Formulae.
justification: Fecal bacterial populations (bifidobacteria, bacteroides, clostridia, lactic acid bacteria) were quantified exclusively by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with Cy3-labeled probes, not sequencing-based taxonomic profiling, across standard formula, three prebiotic-supplemented formula arms, and a breastfed reference group.

title: Effects of Term Infant Formulas Containing High sn-2 Palmitate With and Without Oligofructose on Stool Composition, Stool Characteristics, and Bifidogenicity.
justification: Fecal bifidobacteria were quantified exclusively by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with probe BIF164, not sequencing-based taxonomic profiling, across standard formula, sn-2 palmitate formula (with/without oligofructose), and a human-milk-fed reference group.

title: Bifidobacterium population analysis in the infant gut by direct mapping of genomic hybridization patterns: potential for monitoring temporal development and effects of dietary regimens.
justification: Bifidobacterium composition was assessed using a comparative genome hybridization microarray platform, not DNA sequencing, and the analysis is restricted to within-genus Bifidobacterium species/strain identification rather than overall bacterial taxonomic composition.

title: Growth and safety evaluation of infant formulae containing oligosaccharides derived from bovine milk: a randomized, double-blind, noninferiority trial.
justification: Stool bacterial counts (bifidobacteria, lactobacilli, enterobacteria, clostridia, bacteroides) were quantified by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and culture plating, not sequencing-based taxonomic profiling, across standard formula, BMOS formula, BMOS+probiotic formula, and a breastfed reference group.

title: Association between gut microbiota development and allergy in infants born during pandemic-related social distancing restrictions.
justification: CORAL cohort of term Irish infants (explicit term-only eligibility, multiple births/major anomalies excluded), stool profiled by 16S rRNA sequencing at 6 (n=351) and 12 (n=343) months; breastfeeding was the strongest dietary determinant of microbiota composition at both time points, positively associated with Actinomyces, Bifidobacterium bifidum, and B. infantis/B. breve and negatively with Clostridia and Erysipelotrichia (FDR<0.1).

title: Breast-feeding as 'personalized nutrition'.
justification: This is a theoretical/narrative commentary on breastfeeding as an evolutionary and biosocial phenomenon, with no original subjects, methods, or data.

title: Effect of Pre- and Perinatal Factors and Infant Nutrition on the Intestinal Microbiota.
justification: Explicitly published as an 'Editorial' summarizing five other articles in a Nutrients Special Issue, with no original study subjects or data of its own.

title: Intestinal microbiota and health in infants and children.
justification: This is a narrative commentary discussing HMOs, HMO-analogues, and delivery mode as determinants of infant gut microbiota, synthesizing prior literature with no original subjects or data.

title: A study on the effects of probiotic intervention on growth and development, and normal diseases in children.
justification: This is a clinical trial registry entry (status: Recruiting/Ongoing, submitted 07/11/2025) describing a planned probiotic-intervention trial protocol, not a completed study with reported results.

title: Efficacy and safety of a synbiotic infant formula for the prevention of respiratory and gastrointestinal infections: a randomized controlled trial.
justification: GOLF III study: 460 infants randomized to synbiotic formula (GOS + L. fermentum CECT5716) vs. control formula, both formula arms; the 80-infant human-milk group is a non-randomized reference with no isolable breastfed-vs-unsupplemented-formula microbiome contrast reported. Also independently fails on sequencing: outcomes are infection incidence, fecal pH, and secretory IgA only; no 16S/shotgun/sequencing-based microbiome data anywhere in the document (confirmed via full-text grep for sequencing-related terms).

title: Comparative evaluation of enriched formula milk powder with OPO and MFGM vs. breastfeeding and regular formula milk powder in full-term infants: a comprehensive study on gut microbiota, neurodevelopment, and growth
justification: 3-arm study (breast milk group BMG n=50; regular formula group RFG n=12; OPO/MFGM-fortified formula group FFG n=17) with 16S rRNA (V3-V4, Illumina NovaSeq) gut microbiota profiling in healthy term infants over 1/4/6 months. A direct breastfed-vs-regular-formula contrast (BMG vs. RFG) is isolated and reported throughout (phylum/genus composition, Bifidobacterium/Klebsiella/Veillonella abundance, alpha/beta diversity, PICRUSt2 functional prediction) independent of the additional fortified-formula arm, satisfying PECO.

title: Comparison of the effects of different infant formulas on the growth and development and intestinal flora of infants.
justification: Multicenter study: breastfeeding (BF, non-randomized control) vs. three randomized formula groups (full goat-milk protein, partial goat-milk protein, cow-milk formula) in healthy term infants (enrolled 0-3 months, followed to 6 months). 16S rDNA (V3-V4, Illumina MiSeq) stool microbiota profiling with direct BF-vs-formula comparisons reported (Bifidobacteriaceae relative abundance, alpha/beta diversity, family-level composition correlations). Not a supplement/probiotic exposure -- formulas differ by milk-protein source, not an added probiotic/supplement.

title: Breast milk urea as a nitrogen source for urease positive Bifidobacterium infantis.
justification: Combines in vitro B. infantis urease physiology (pure-culture growth/enzymatic assays, proteomics) with a shotgun-metagenomic reanalysis of pooled public infant gut datasets (92 samples/74 healthy term infants, <=6 months, solely breastfed or solely formula-fed, antibiotic/preterm/diseased excluded) showing a 2.3-fold higher abundance of urease-related genes in breastfed vs. formula-fed infants. The human metagenome component is a genuine sequencing-based functional BF-vs-FF comparison satisfying PECO; the in vitro portion is supplementary mechanistic support, not the whole study. CONFIRMED COHORT-OVERLAP NOTE: the pooled metagenome data draw on three source studies (Schwartz 2012, Yatsunenko 2012, Valles 2014). Checked against the corpus: Schwartz 2012 IS separately included (covidence #2022, Include), and a third paper reanalyzing that same Schwartz dataset (covidence #3324) was already excluded here as 'Duplicate report of an already-included cohort' since it added no new primary data. Yatsunenko 2012 and Valles 2014 do not appear elsewhere in this corpus. Unlike #3324, this paper (a) pools three cohorts rather than reanalyzing Schwartz's data alone, (b) reports a genuinely novel finding (urease-gene abundance) absent from Schwartz 2012/#2022 itself, and (c) is majority original in vitro bacteriology, not a reanalysis paper -- kept as Include, but review team should confirm this distinction is acceptable at synthesis stage given the partial sample overlap with #2022.

title: Randomized controlled trial on the impact of early-life intervention with bifidobacteria on the healthy infant fecal microbiota and metabolome.
justification: Double-blind RCT: bifidobacteria-supplemented formula (F+, n=48) vs. unsupplemented placebo formula (F-, n=49), with an exclusively-breastfed reference group (B, n=9) followed over 12 (and partly 24) months. Unlike a supplement-only comparison, the plain breastfed-vs-unsupplemented-formula contrast IS isolated and extensively reported as its own result (beta-diversity, richness/Shannon diversity, phylum/OTU-level taxa including B. longum and R. gnavus, SCFA profiles, Figs 2-5, Table 1) -- satisfies the carve-out in criterion 3. 16S rRNA (V3-V4, Illumina MiSeq) plus UHPLC-MS metabolomics (functional secondary outcome); healthy term infants; stool samples.

title: Host-Microbe Interactions in the Neonatal Intestine: Role of Human Milk Oligosaccharides
justification: Donovan et al., Advances in Nutrition conference supplement (First International Conference on Glycobiology of Human Milk Oligosaccharides, 2011). Explicitly self-described by the authors as a review ("In this review, the current evidence linking HMO to host-microbe interactions in the infant gut is discussed..."), structured with thematic review headers rather than IMRaD, and the BF-vs-FF 16S phylum data shown (Fig. 3) are illustrative preliminary figures from an ongoing pilot study with no dedicated Methods section (sample size, recruitment, statistics) -- not a full primary-study report.

title: Stool microbiota in term infants fed formula supplemented with human milk oligosaccharides (HMOS: 2'fucosyllactose and lacto-n-neotetraose) and reduced likelihood of antibiotic use
justification: Conference abstract (Berger et al. 2016; citation format '175(11):1505', single page, DOI shared with the whole supplement issue rather than unique to this abstract -- the same DOI is shared with covidence #10423, confirming both are entries from the same conference abstract book). No full-length peer-reviewed article identified. Decided without full text: full text does not exist for a conference abstract.

title: New formula supplemented with milk fat globule membrane and synbiotics modulates the gut microbiota and reduces illness symptoms during infancy
justification: Conference abstract (Campoy et al. 2018; citation format '73():73', single page number, typical of an annual-meeting abstract supplement). No full-length peer-reviewed article identified. Decided without full text: full text does not exist for a conference abstract.

title: The norwegian preterm infant gut (PINGU) multicenter study: gut microbiota composition and early impact of probiotic treatment
justification: Conference abstract (Esaiassen et al. 2016; citation format '175(11):1516', shares its DOI with covidence #10139, confirming both are entries from the same conference abstract supplement). Independently also fails on population: cohort is 33 infants <28wk gestation + 33 infants 29-31wk gestation (preterm, probiotic-supplemented vs not), with only 10 term breastfed infants as a small reference group -- no separable healthy-term comparison of adequate size. Decided without full text: full text does not exist for a conference abstract.

title: Beneficial effects of human milk and prebiotic-like fermented infant formulas on the intestinal microflora and immune system
justification: Book chapter (Mullie, Izard & Romond 2010, in 'Milk Consumption and Health', pp. 215-248) -- the abstract itself states 'We will first review the beneficial effects of mother's milk...we will focus on prebiotics...we will compare the effect of this formula...', explicitly framing it as a narrative review, not original research. Decided on abstract; full text not pursued given the review framing is unambiguous.

title: Immunity Modification of Full Term Infants According to the Type of Feeding and Mode of Delivery
justification: ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry (NCT03637894, registered 2018), not a published article. The Covidence 'abstract' is the registry's study description/protocol (methods, planned analyses, sample-size calculation) with no results reported. Decided without full text: a trial registration has none to retrieve.

title: Immunity Modification of Full Term Infants According to the Type of Feeding and Mode of Delivery
justification: ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry (NCT04256356, registered 2020) -- a follow-on dose-response phase of the same protocol as covidence #10451 (identical title). Registry description only, no results reported. Decided without full text: a trial registration has none to retrieve.

title: Efficacy of Two HMOs in Chinese Infants
justification: ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry (NCT06361719, registered 2024). Registry description only ('This is a randomized, controlled, double-blind, intervention trial...to evaluate the efficacy...'), no results reported. Decided without full text: a trial registration has none to retrieve.

title: HMOs on Infant Gut Microbiota Modulation and Development of the Immune System in Healthy Infants
justification: ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry (NCT06631937, registered 2024). Registry description only, no results reported ('The goal of this clinical trial is to learn how...'). Decided without full text: a trial registration has none to retrieve.

title: Goat Milk-Derived Formula vs. Undiluted Goat Milk in Infants Unable to Exclusively Breastfeed: growth and Biomarker Analysis
justification: ClinicalTrials.gov registry entry (NCT07225153, registered 2025). Registry description only, written in future tense ('This community-based randomized controlled trial will evaluate...'), no results reported. Decided without full text: a trial registration has none to retrieve.

title: HUMAN MILK OLIGOSACCHARIDES AND INFANT FORMULA.
justification: No abstract available in Covidence; authors listed as '[Unknown authors]'; single-page item (Nutrition Today 2024;59(3):83-83) -- format strongly indicates a brief news/commentary note rather than a primary research article. LOWER CONFIDENCE than other rows in this batch since no abstract exists to directly confirm; based on title, authorship, and page-length pattern only.

title: Mothers, babies and friendly bacteria
justification: No abstract available in Covidence. Title and journal section (Archives of Disease in Childhood - Fetal and Neonatal Edition, 2011) strongly suggest a commentary/perspective piece rather than original research. LOWER CONFIDENCE than other rows in this batch since no abstract exists to directly confirm; based on title and journal context only.

title: The Impact of the Human Milk Microbiota in the Prevention of Disease and Infant Health.
justification: No abstract available in Covidence. Title ('The Impact of...in the Prevention of Disease and Infant Health') and 17-page span (Breastfeeding Medicine 2023;18(6):413-430) are characteristic of a narrative review rather than a primary research report. LOWER CONFIDENCE than other rows in this batch since no abstract exists to directly confirm; based on title and page-length pattern only.

title: Breastfeeding promotes early neonatal regulatory T-cell expansion and immune tolerance of non-inherited maternal antigens.
justification: Wood et al. 2021, Allergy. Primarily an immunology study (Treg expansion, mixed lymphocyte reactions) in 38 term caesarean-delivered infant-mother dyads, but directly compares infant stool microbiome by feeding group (exclusively breastfed vs. mixed vs. exclusively formula-fed) via 16S rRNA V4 sequencing (QIIME2/Silva) at 3 weeks of age: alpha/beta diversity showed no difference, but LEfSe and random-forest analysis found Veillonella and Gemella enriched in breastfed infants. Healthy term infants (elective c-section, no labor), genuine BF-vs-FF stool comparison, sequencing-based. Flagged by the original fork batch as 'unscreenable' but later confirmed by full-document contamination audit to have correct, uncorrupted content -- simply never actually screened until now.

title: Probiotic Intervention Through the Pregnant and Breastfeeding Mother to Reduce Disease Risk in the Child
justification: Rautava 2018, Breastfeeding Medicine 13(S1):S14-S15 -- a short single-author narrative commentary in a conference-supplement issue (note the 'S1' supplement number and two-page span), summarizing the author's own and others' prior published studies on maternal probiotic supplementation during pregnancy/breastfeeding. No new Methods or Results section, no original cohort or primary data of its own. Flagged by the original fork batch as 'unscreenable' but later confirmed by full-document contamination audit to have correct, uncorrupted content -- simply never actually screened until now.

title: Influence of Early Life Factors, including breast milk Composition, on the Microbiome of Infants Born to Mothers with and without Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
justification: Sabino et al. 2023, MECONIUM cohort. 294 infants (80 born to mothers with IBD, 214-216 to non-IBD mothers), 1034 fecal samples, 16S rRNA V3-V4 (DADA2/Silva v132). Cohort includes both IBD-exposed and healthy-mother infants; the infants themselves are healthy (none developed IBD). Maternal IBD is a studied covariate/stratifier, not a clinical condition defining the infant cohort (criterion 5 concerns the infant's own condition). Reports an explicit, adjusted breastfed-vs-formula-fed comparison independent of maternal IBD status: Staphylococcus higher in exclusively breastfed infants, Enterococcus higher in formula-fed (p=0.04), Intestinibacter significantly higher in exclusively formula-fed infants (p=7.3x10-8) after adjusting for delivery mode and maternal IBD diagnosis.

title: Effect of Delivery Mode and Nutrition on Gut Microbiota in Neonates.
justification: Akagawa et al. 2019. 36 healthy full-term Japanese neonates (NICU admissions explicitly excluded), 4 groups by delivery mode x feeding type (VD/BF, VD/FF, CD/BF, CD/FF), stool at 4 days and 1 month, 16S rRNA sequencing (Ion PGM), order-level composition and Shannon diversity. Reports an explicit (null) feeding-type comparison: 'no significant differences in gut microbiota according to the feeding type.' Note for extraction/synthesis: the 'FF' group was classified as >80% formula rather than exclusive -- all 16 FF-classified neonates received some breastmilk -- which may explain the null result; relevant to RQ1 (method-dependence) and RQ4 (exposure-definition comparability).

title: Association of Cesarean Delivery and Formula Supplementation With the Intestinal Microbiome of 6-Week-Old Infants.
justification: Madan et al. 2016, JAMA Pediatrics. 102 healthy full-term infants (>37 weeks, appropriate growth, antibiotic-exposed infants excluded), stool at ~6 weeks, three feeding groups (exclusively breastfed n=70, combination-fed n=26, exclusively formula-fed n=6), 16S rRNA V4-V5 sequencing, generalized UniFrac community analysis plus genus-level differential abundance (Lactococcus significantly depleted in exclusively breastfed vs. exclusively formula-fed, p<.001, Q=.002). Clean, well-powered, explicit breastfed-vs-formula comparison independent of and adjusted for delivery mode.

title: Comparison of gut microbiome and metabolome characteristics in preterm and full-term infants under different feeding modes
justification: Yin et al. 2026, Acta Microbiologica Sinica. 4 groups (n=10 each): breastfeeding/non-breastfeeding preterm (29-36wk) and breastfeeding/non-breastfeeding full-term (37-42wk) infants, all vaginally delivered (controlling for delivery mode). 'Non-breastfeeding' explicitly defined as exclusively formula-fed, excluding mixed feeding. 16S rRNA V3-V4 (QIIME2/DADA2/Silva138) plus untargeted metabolomics. The full-term breastfed (BTI) vs. full-term formula-fed (NBTI) comparison is cleanly separable from the preterm arms per criterion 4's 'separable healthy-term subgroup' allowance: Bifidobacterium 45.98% in BTI (p<0.0005 vs. other groups) vs. Enterococcus-dominant (59.20%) in NBTI, LEfSe-confirmed differential taxa. EXTRACTION NOTE: restrict extraction to the BTI vs. NBTI (full-term) subgroup only, excluding the BPI/NBPI preterm data. Small sample size (n=10/group); authors describe this as a pioneering exploratory study with no strict causal inference -- flag for risk-of-bias assessment.

title: Stunted microbiota and opportunistic pathogen colonization in caesarean-section birth.
justification: Shao et al. 2019, Nature (Baby Biome Study). 596 healthy full-term infants (39.5+/-1.37 weeks gestation), 1679 longitudinal shotgun metagenomic samples from UK hospitals. Delivery mode is the primary focus, but breastfeeding is explicitly analyzed and reported as an independent covariate via PERMANOVA and MaAsLin: 'the absence of breastfeeding during the neonatal period was associated with a higher carriage of C. perfringens, K. oxytoca and E. faecalis.' Large, high-quality shotgun metagenomic study with a genuine, quantified breastfed-vs-not finding independent of delivery mode.
